section-91: 1857: causes included Dalhousie's annexations (Doctrine of Lapse, Awadh 1856), economic distress of peasants, artisans and taluqdars, fear of religious interference, the grievances of sepoys (low pay, overseas service, discrimination) and the greased cartridges. It began at Meerut (10 May 1857) and spread to Delhi, Kanpur, Lucknow, Jhansi, Bareilly, Bihar and central India, led by Bahadur Shah Zafar, Nana Saheb, Tantia Tope, Rani Lakshmibai, Begum Hazrat Mahal and Kunwar Singh. It failed due to lack of unity, planning and modern weapons, the loyalty of Punjab, Bengal and the south, the support of many princes for the British and superior British resources. It led to Crown rule (1858), the reorganisation of the army (more European troops, recruitment of 'martial races') and a policy of non-interference and alliance with princes and landlords.

Congress and the Moderates (1885-1905): the founding of the Congress followed earlier associations (the British Indian Association, Indian Association, Poona Sarvajanik Sabha, Madras Mahajan Sabha). The Moderates built national consciousness through the economic critique of colonialism (Naoroji, R. C. Dutt, Ranade), demands for constitutional reforms and civil rights, and constitutional methods. The Extremists (Tilak, Lajpat Rai, Pal, Aurobindo) demanded swaraj and mass action.

Partition of Bengal and Swadeshi (1905-1908): Curzon's partition aimed to weaken Bengali nationalism and divide Hindus and Muslims. The Swadeshi movement used boycott, swadeshi enterprises, national education, samitis and cultural revival (Tagore). It spread nationalism to new groups and areas, but its limited appeal to Muslim peasants, the Surat split (1907) and repression led to its decline; some youth turned to revolutionary terrorism (the Anushilan Samiti, Jugantar; Khudiram Bose). The partition was annulled in 1911.
section-92: Home Rule: Tilak's and Besant's Leagues (1916) mobilised opinion through propaganda and organisation, paving the way for the Lucknow Pact (1916) and the Montagu Declaration (1917), and preparing a new generation of activists for Gandhian politics. Communal politics: the Muslim League (1906) and separate electorates (1909), the Hindu Mahasabha and RSS, communal riots in the 1920s, and later the Lahore Resolution (1940) and two-nation theory led towards Partition. Historians (Bipan Chandra) argue that communalism was a modern phenomenon encouraged by colonial policy and middle-class competition.

The left: the CPI (1920/1925), trade unions and kisan sabhas, the CSP (1934), and leftist leaders like Nehru and Bose pushed Congress towards socialist and pro-peasant programmes. Revolutionaries: the Ghadar Party (1913), the HRA/HSRA (Ram Prasad Bismil, Ashfaqulla Khan, Kakori conspiracy 1925; Chandrashekhar Azad, Bhagat Singh), and the Chittagong group of Surya Sen; they inspired youth though their methods differed from Gandhi's.

Final phase: the INA under Subhas Chandra Bose fought with Japan (Imphal-Kohima, 1944) and the INA trials (1945-1946) generated huge public support. The RIN Mutiny (February 1946) and strikes in the air force and army showed that Britain could no longer rely on Indian armed forces. Combined with economic exhaustion after the Second World War and the Labour government's attitude, these events made British withdrawal inevitable.
section-93: Gandhi's methods: satyagraha (non-violent resistance based on truth), non-cooperation, civil disobedience, fasting and constructive programmes (khadi, village industries, Hindu-Muslim unity, removal of untouchability, prohibition). His early campaigns in Champaran, Kheda and Ahmedabad (1917-1918) and the Rowlatt satyagraha (1919) established him as a mass leader. His use of simple symbols (spinning wheel, salt) and Indian languages connected with peasants and ordinary people.

Non-Cooperation and Khilafat (1920-1922): boycott of councils, courts, schools and foreign goods; national schools; the spread of nationalism to towns and villages; Hindu-Muslim unity; and withdrawal after Chauri Chaura. Civil Disobedience (1930-1934): Purna Swaraj, the Salt March, breaking of salt, forest and tax laws, the Gandhi-Irwin Pact and Round Table Conferences; wider participation of women, peasants and the frontier (Khudai Khidmatgars), though Muslim participation was lower. Quit India (1942): 'Do or Die', immediate arrest of leaders, spontaneous mass uprising, parallel governments and severe repression.

Evaluation: Gandhi made nationalism a mass movement and gave it a moral and non-violent character. Critics point to his sudden withdrawals of movements, his compromise with landlords and capitalists (according to Marxist historians), his religious idiom (which some argue alienated Muslims) and his conflict with Ambedkar over separate electorates (Poona Pact, 1932). Each movement nevertheless weakened British authority and widened the social base of nationalism.
section-94: 1919-1935: the Montagu-Chelmsford reforms (Government of India Act 1919) introduced dyarchy in the provinces. The all-white Simon Commission (1927) was boycotted, and the Nehru Report (1928) proposed an Indian constitution with dominion status and fundamental rights. The three Round Table Conferences (1930-1932) and the Communal Award (1932) led to the Government of India Act 1935, which provided for provincial autonomy and an all-India federation (never implemented). Congress ministries were formed in 1937 in most provinces but resigned in 1939 when India was taken into the war without consultation.

War years: the August Offer (1940) and the Cripps Mission (1942) failed; the Quit India movement followed. After the war, the Wavell Plan and Simla Conference (1945) failed over the League's claim to represent all Muslims; the elections of 1945-1946 showed the Congress dominant in general seats and the League in Muslim seats. The Cabinet Mission Plan (1946) proposed a united India with groupings; disagreement and the League's Direct Action Day (16 August 1946) led to communal violence. An interim government and the Constituent Assembly (December 1946) were formed.

Independence and Partition: Attlee's announcement (February 1947), Mountbatten's 3 June Plan, and the Indian Independence Act (July 1947) created India and Pakistan on 14-15 August 1947. Partition led to massive violence and migration. The Constituent Assembly, chaired by Rajendra Prasad with Ambedkar as Chairman of the Drafting Committee, framed the Constitution, adopted on 26 November 1949 and in force from 26 January 1950.
section-98: After Vasco da Gama's arrival at Calicut (1498), the Portuguese built their 'Estado da India'. Francisco de Almeida (1505-1509) pursued naval dominance and defeated a combined Egyptian-Gujarati fleet at Diu (1509). Afonso de Albuquerque (1509-1515) captured Goa (1510), Malacca (1511) and Hormuz (1515), controlling key points of Indian Ocean trade; he encouraged Portuguese marriages with local women. Nino da Cunha acquired Diu and Bassein from Gujarat.

The Portuguese used the cartaz (pass) system and forced Asian traders to pay customs at their ports. They spread Catholicism (the Jesuit Francis Xavier; the Goa Inquisition from 1560), introduced tobacco, chilli, potato, maize, cashew and pineapple, and the printing press (1556). Their decline resulted from competition with the Dutch and English, religious intolerance, corruption, the small population of Portugal and its union with Spain (1580-1640). They lost Hooghly to the Mughals (1632) but held Goa, Daman and Diu until 1961.
section-99: The Dutch East India Company (Vereenigde Oostindische Compagnie, VOC) was formed in 1602. Its main interest was the spice trade of the Indonesian islands; in India it sought textiles to exchange for spices. It established factories at Masulipatnam (1605), Pulicat (1610, its main base on the Coromandel coast, later Negapatnam), Surat (1616), Chinsura (Bengal, 1653), Kasimbazar, Patna, Balasore and Cochin (captured from the Portuguese, 1663).

The Dutch exported Indian textiles, indigo, saltpetre, raw silk and opium. Their power in India declined after the English defeated them at the Battle of Chinsura or Bidara (1759), and they concentrated on Indonesia. An Anglo-Dutch agreement (1667) had already given the Dutch the Indonesian islands while the English focused on India.
section-100: The French East India Company (Compagnie des Indes Orientales) was founded in 1664 under Colbert, minister of Louis XIV; it was a state-controlled company. François Caron set up the first factory at Surat (1668); Masulipatnam followed (1669). François Martin founded Pondicherry (1674), which became the headquarters; other settlements were Chandernagore (Bengal, 1690), Mahe, Karaikal and Yanam.

Under Governor-General Joseph François Dupleix (1742-1754), the French began interfering in Indian politics to gain territory and revenue, using trained Indian soldiers (sepoys) and supporting rival claimants to thrones. This led to the Carnatic Wars with the English. The French were finally defeated at Wandiwash (1760) and lost Pondicherry (1761), though it was returned and remained French until 1954.
section-101: The English East India Company received a charter from Queen Elizabeth I on 31 December 1600 for trade in the East. Captain William Hawkins visited Jahangir's court (1608); after the English defeated the Portuguese at Swally (1612), Jahangir allowed a factory at Surat (1613). Sir Thomas Roe, ambassador of James I, obtained further privileges (1615-1619). The Company acquired Madras (Fort St George, 1639-1640), Bombay (received from Charles II, who got it as dowry from Portugal, 1668) and Calcutta (founded by Job Charnock, 1690; Fort William, 1696).

The Mughal emperor Farrukhsiyar's farman (1717) gave the Company duty-free trade in Bengal in exchange for a yearly payment, which led to misuse of dastaks (passes) by Company servants. In the eighteenth century, the Company became a political and military power through wars in the Carnatic and Bengal, gradually transforming into a territorial ruler.
section-102: The English and French companies competed for trade in South India and in Bengal. Their rivalry was linked to European wars: the War of the Austrian Succession (1740-1748), the Seven Years' War (1756-1763) and later the American War of Independence and Napoleonic Wars. Both used the disputes of Indian rulers over succession to gain influence, supporting rival claimants in Hyderabad and the Carnatic.

The English won because of their stronger navy, better financial resources (Bengal's revenue after Plassey), the support of the British government, better commanders (Clive, Eyre Coote) and the recall of Dupleix (1754). The French company was state-controlled and poorly supported. The French continued to help Indian rulers (Haidar Ali, Tipu Sultan, the Marathas) against the English, but never recovered their power.
section-103: Hyderabad was founded as an autonomous state in 1724 by Mir Qamaruddin Khan Siddiqi, known as Chin Qilich Khan and Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I, a powerful Mughal noble and viceroy of the Deccan. After defeating the Mughal governor at Shakar Kheda (1724), he ruled practically independently while acknowledging the Mughal emperor formally. His dynasty, the Asaf Jahis (Nizams), ruled until 1948.

Hyderabad faced pressure from the Marathas (who extracted chauth), the English and the French. After Nizam-ul-Mulk's death (1748), a succession dispute between Nasir Jang and Muzaffar Jang involved the English and French in the Second Carnatic War. The Nizam later signed the Subsidiary Alliance (1798) with Wellesley. Hyderabad was the largest princely state in India and was integrated into India in 1948 by 'Operation Polo'.
section-104: First Carnatic War (1746-1748): part of the War of the Austrian Succession. The French under La Bourdonnais captured Madras (1746); Dupleix defeated the army of the Nawab of the Carnatic, Anwaruddin, at St Thome (Adyar, 1746), showing the superiority of trained European troops. The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748) restored Madras to the English.

Second Carnatic War (1749-1754): over succession disputes in Hyderabad (Nasir Jang vs Muzaffar Jang) and the Carnatic (Anwaruddin's son Muhammad Ali vs Chanda Sahib). The French supported Muzaffar Jang and Chanda Sahib; the English supported their rivals. Robert Clive's capture and defence of Arcot (1751) turned the war in the English favour; Muhammad Ali became Nawab. Dupleix was recalled in 1754. Third Carnatic War (1756-1763): part of the Seven Years' War. The French under Count de Lally lost to Sir Eyre Coote at Wandiwash (1760), and Pondicherry fell (1761). The Treaty of Paris (1763) returned Pondicherry but forbade French fortifications, ending French political ambitions in India.
section-105: Siraj-ud-Daulah, Nawab of Bengal (1756), opposed the English fortification of Calcutta, the misuse of dastaks and their sheltering of his enemies. He captured Calcutta (1756); the 'Black Hole' incident (the alleged death of English prisoners in a small room) was used for propaganda. Robert Clive recaptured Calcutta and conspired with Mir Jafar (the Nawab's commander), Jagat Seth (bankers) and others. At the Battle of Plassey (23 June 1757), Mir Jafar's betrayal led to Siraj's defeat. Mir Jafar became Nawab and paid huge sums to the Company and its officers.

Mir Qasim (1760-1763), who replaced Mir Jafar, tried to assert independence, moving his capital to Monghyr and abolishing internal duties for everyone. He was defeated, and allied with Shuja-ud-Daulah of Awadh and Mughal emperor Shah Alam II; their combined army lost at Buxar (22 October 1764). By the Treaty of Allahabad (1765), Shah Alam granted the Company the diwani (right to collect revenue) of Bengal, Bihar and Odisha. Bengal's wealth gave the Company resources for further expansion.
section-106: Haidar Ali, a soldier who rose to control the Wodeyar kingdom of Mysore (1761), built a modern army with French help. In the First Anglo-Mysore War (1767-1769), he forced the English to sign the Treaty of Madras on his terms. In the Second (1780-1784), he defeated the English but died in 1782; his son Tipu Sultan concluded the Treaty of Mangalore (1784).

Tipu Sultan (1782-1799), the 'Tiger of Mysore', introduced a new calendar, coinage, weights and measures, promoted trade and industry, planted a 'Tree of Liberty' and joined the Jacobin Club in Seringapatam, and sought help from France and the Ottomans. He used iron-cased rockets in battle. In the Third War (1790-1792), Cornwallis allied with the Marathas and the Nizam and forced Tipu to cede half his territory (Treaty of Seringapatam). In the Fourth War (1799), Wellesley's forces stormed Seringapatam; Tipu died fighting. The Wodeyars were restored under a Subsidiary Alliance.
section-107: The Maratha confederacy after Panipat (1761) was led by the Peshwa at Pune and great chiefs - the Gaekwad (Baroda), Holkar (Indore), Sindhia (Gwalior) and Bhonsle (Nagpur). The First Anglo-Maratha War (1775-1782) arose from the English support for Raghunath Rao's claim to the Peshwaship; the Marathas, guided by Nana Phadnavis and Mahadji Sindhia, held their own, and the Treaty of Salbai (1782) restored the status quo.

After Nana Phadnavis's death (1800), internal conflict led Peshwa Baji Rao II to sign the Treaty of Bassein (1802), accepting a Subsidiary Alliance. This caused the Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803-1805), in which Wellesley and Lake defeated Sindhia and Bhonsle (battles of Assaye, Laswari). The Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817-1818) under Lord Hastings ended Maratha power: the Peshwa's territories were annexed, Baji Rao II was pensioned off at Bithur, and a small state at Satara was created for Shivaji's descendants.
section-108: Ranjit Singh (1780-1839) united the Sikh misls, captured Lahore (1799) and Amritsar, and built a powerful kingdom including Kashmir, Multan and Peshawar. He modernised his army (the Fauj-i-Khas) with European officers, maintained friendly relations with the British (Treaty of Amritsar, 1809, fixing the Sutlej as the boundary) and obtained the Koh-i-Noor diamond.

After his death, instability, palace intrigues and the power of the army (Khalsa) led to wars with the British. The First Anglo-Sikh War (1845-1846; Mudki, Ferozeshah, Aliwal, Sobraon) ended with the Treaty of Lahore, ceding territory (Jalandhar Doab; Kashmir sold to Gulab Singh). The Second Anglo-Sikh War (1848-1849; Chillianwala, Gujrat) led Dalhousie to annex Punjab in 1849. The young Maharaja Duleep Singh was sent to England and the Koh-i-Noor was taken to Queen Victoria.
section-109: Awadh became an autonomous state under Saadat Khan Burhan-ul-Mulk (1722). After Buxar (1764), Shuja-ud-Daulah became an ally of the Company, paying for British troops. The Nawabs' financial burden increased under Warren Hastings (who pressured the Begums of Awadh to give up their treasure) and Wellesley (1801 treaty, by which the Nawab ceded half his territory, including Rohilkhand and the Doab).

Awadh was known for its rich culture in Lucknow (the Bara Imambara, Lucknowi tehzeeb, Urdu poetry, music and dance). Dalhousie annexed it in February 1856 on grounds of 'misgovernment', exiling Nawab Wajid Ali Shah to Calcutta. The annexation angered taluqdars, soldiers (many sepoys came from Awadh) and common people, making Awadh a major centre of the 1857 revolt under Begum Hazrat Mahal.
section-110: Developed by Lord Wellesley (Governor-General, 1798-1805), though the French Dupleix had used similar ideas. Under it, an Indian ruler had to: accept a British army stationed in his territory and pay for it (in cash or by ceding territory); accept a British Resident at his court; not employ other Europeans without British approval; not make war or alliances with other states without British consent; and in return, the British would protect him from external and internal enemies.

The first to accept was the Nizam of Hyderabad (1798); others included Mysore (1799), Tanjore (1799), Awadh (1801), the Peshwa (1802), Bhonsle and Sindhia (1803). Effects: rulers lost independence, became financially burdened, often neglected administration, and many disbanded their armies, leaving soldiers unemployed. The British gained a large army paid for by Indian states, control over foreign affairs and an excuse to annex states that failed to pay.
section-111: Lord Dalhousie (Governor-General, 1848-1856) applied the Doctrine of Lapse: if a ruler of a dependent state died without a natural male heir, the state would 'lapse' to the Company, and adoption of an heir would not be recognised without permission. States annexed included Satara (1848), Jaitpur and Sambalpur (1849), Baghat (1850), Udaipur (Chhattisgarh, 1852), Jhansi (1853) and Nagpur (1854).

Dalhousie also abolished titles and pensions, such as Nana Saheb's pension as the adopted son of Baji Rao II. The policy created deep resentment among Indian rulers and their subjects. Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi, whose adopted son was not recognised, and Nana Saheb became important leaders of 1857. After 1857, Queen Victoria's Proclamation abandoned the Doctrine of Lapse and recognised the right of adoption.
section-112: After obtaining the diwani in 1765, Clive introduced the Dual System of Government in Bengal (1765-1772). The Company had the diwani (revenue collection and civil justice), while the Nawab retained the nizamat (police, criminal justice and administration). In practice, the Company appointed deputy diwans (Muhammad Reza Khan for Bengal, Shitab Rai for Bihar) to collect revenue, and also controlled the deputy nazim.

Thus the Company had power without responsibility, while the Nawab had responsibility without power. The result was misgovernment, oppressive revenue collection, corruption among Company servants and the ruin of Bengal's economy and artisans. The terrible Bengal famine of 1770 killed about a third of the population. Warren Hastings abolished the system in 1772, and the Company took direct charge of administration.
section-113: The Regulating Act was passed by the British Parliament under Prime Minister Lord North in 1773, after the Company faced financial crisis and reports of corruption. It was the first step towards parliamentary control over the Company. The Governor of Bengal became the Governor-General of Bengal (Warren Hastings was the first), with a council of four members, and the governors of Bombay and Madras were made subordinate to him in matters of war and peace.

A Supreme Court was established at Calcutta (1774) with a chief justice (Elijah Impey) and three judges. Company servants were prohibited from private trade and accepting bribes or gifts. The Court of Directors had to submit reports on revenue, civil and military affairs to the government. Defects: the Governor-General could be outvoted by his council; the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and the council was unclear; and the presidencies' subordination was ineffective. These defects led to the Act of 1781 and Pitt's India Act.
section-114: Pitt's India Act (1784), passed under Prime Minister William Pitt the Younger, created a dual system of control: the Court of Directors managed commercial affairs, while a Board of Control (six members, including the Chancellor of the Exchequer and a Secretary of State) supervised civil, military and revenue affairs. The Company's territories in India were called 'British possessions in India' for the first time.

The Governor-General's council was reduced to three members; the Governor-General was given control over Bombay and Madras in matters of war, revenue and diplomacy. The Act of 1786 allowed Cornwallis to override his council and to be also Commander-in-Chief. The system of dual control lasted until 1858, when the Crown took over directly.
section-115: Charter Act of 1793: renewed the Company's charter and trade monopoly for twenty years; strengthened the powers of the Governor-General over the council and presidencies; salaries of the Board of Control were paid from Indian revenues. Charter Act of 1813: ended the Company's trade monopoly in India (except for tea and trade with China); allowed Christian missionaries to enter India; and allocated one lakh rupees annually for education - the first commitment to education.

Charter Act of 1833: ended the Company's commercial functions entirely, making it a purely administrative body; the Governor-General of Bengal became the Governor-General of India (William Bentinck was the first), with full legislative powers for the whole country; a law member (Macaulay) was added to the council; and it declared that no Indian would be denied office due to religion, birth or colour. Charter Act of 1853: separated the legislative and executive functions of the council, created a legislative council, introduced open competition for the civil service (the Indian Civil Service), and did not renew the charter for a fixed period, foreshadowing the end of Company rule.
section-116: Political causes: aggressive annexations (Doctrine of Lapse, annexation of Awadh), the humiliation of the Mughal emperor (Dalhousie and Canning announced that Bahadur Shah's successors would lose the title and palace), and the loss of power and pensions of rulers and nobles. Economic causes: high land revenue and the loss of land by peasants and taluqdars (especially in Awadh under the Summary Settlement, 1856); ruin of artisans by British imports; unemployment of soldiers and officials of annexed states.

Social and religious causes: fear of Christian conversion (missionary activities, the Religious Disabilities Act 1850, which allowed converts to inherit), social reforms (abolition of sati, Widow Remarriage Act 1856), Western education and railways and telegraphs seen as threats to caste and religion, and British racial arrogance. Military causes: low pay and limited promotion for Indian sepoys; withdrawal of allowances (bhatta) for service outside their areas; the General Service Enlistment Act (1856); the British army's reverses in the Crimean and Afghan wars; and the immediate cause, the greased cartridges of the new Enfield rifle, which had to be bitten open and were rumoured to contain cow and pig fat.
section-117: Interpretations: (1) a 'sepoy mutiny', according to British officials like John Seeley and some Indian contemporaries; (2) a 'national war of independence', according to V. D. Savarkar ('The Indian War of Independence of 1857', 1909); (3) a feudal reaction by dispossessed rulers and landlords trying to restore the old order, according to some historians (R. C. Majumdar argued it was 'neither first, nor national, nor war of independence'); (4) a 'conspiracy' of Muslims to restore Mughal rule, an old British view now rejected; (5) a combination of military revolt and popular uprising, as argued by S. N. Sen and Eric Stokes, who showed the role of peasants.

Recent historians (Rudrangshu Mukherjee on Awadh, Ranajit Guha and the Subaltern school) emphasise the participation of peasants and the rural population, especially in Awadh and western Bihar, where the revolt became a widespread civil rebellion, with Hindus and Muslims fighting together. Its character varied by region. Most agree it was the most serious challenge to British rule in the nineteenth century, whatever label is used.
section-118: Reasons for failure: (1) limited spread - the revolt was concentrated in north and central India; Punjab, Bengal, the south and most of western India remained quiet; (2) many rulers (Sindhia, Holkar, the Nizam, the Sikh chiefs, the Rana of Nepal) supported the British; (3) lack of central leadership, coordination and common programme - leaders fought for local aims; Bahadur Shah was old and weak; (4) inferior arms and organisation against British rifles, artillery and the telegraph, which allowed rapid communication; (5) British resources from the empire, including troops from Britain and those diverted from China.

In addition, the educated middle class, merchants and moneylenders mostly did not support the revolt, and British commanders such as Colin Campbell, Hugh Rose, Henry Havelock and John Nicholson were able. Delhi was recaptured in September 1857, Lucknow and Kanpur in 1858, and Rani Lakshmibai died fighting at Gwalior (June 1858). Tantia Tope was captured and hanged (1859). The British took brutal revenge, including mass executions.
section-119: The Government of India Act 1858 transferred power from the Company to the Crown. A Secretary of State for India (with a council of fifteen members) in London became responsible for Indian affairs, and the Governor-General became the Viceroy (Canning was the first). Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1 November 1858) announced the end of annexations, respect for treaties with princes and their right to adopt heirs, non-interference in religion, equal protection of the law and a general amnesty.

Military reorganisation: the ratio of European to Indian soldiers was increased; artillery was kept in European hands; recruitment shifted to 'martial races' (Sikhs, Gurkhas, Pathans) from areas loyal in 1857, and regiments were mixed to prevent unity ('divide and rule'). Other effects: the British became allies of princes and landlords; social reforms slowed; racial distance between rulers and ruled widened; and the policy of divide and rule between Hindus and Muslims began. The Mughal dynasty ended with Bahadur Shah Zafar's exile to Rangoon.
section-121: European arrival: the Portuguese (1498) built a maritime empire based on Goa and the cartaz system; the Dutch (VOC, 1602) concentrated on spices and textiles, with bases at Pulicat and Chinsura, and were displaced in India after Bidara (1759); the English (1600) established Surat, Madras, Bombay and Calcutta and gained privileges from the Mughals; the French (1664) established Pondicherry and Chandernagore. The Danes also had settlements (Tranquebar, Serampore).

Carnatic Wars: in the First (1746-1748), the French took Madras and Dupleix defeated the Nawab, showing the strength of European-trained troops; in the Second (1749-1754), the companies backed rival claimants in Hyderabad and the Carnatic, and Clive's seizure of Arcot (1751) led to English success; in the Third (1756-1763), Eyre Coote defeated Lally at Wandiwash (1760) and Pondicherry fell.

Reasons for English success: naval superiority, financial strength (especially Bengal's revenues after Plassey), the private character and commercial efficiency of the English company compared with the state-controlled French company, consistent support from the British government, able leaders, and Dupleix's recall. The Carnatic Wars taught the English how to use Indian political divisions and trained sepoys to gain power - lessons applied in Bengal.
section-122: Bengal: Plassey (1757) made the Company the kingmaker in Bengal; Buxar (1764) and the Treaty of Allahabad (1765) gave it the diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Odisha. Bengal's resources financed later wars. Mysore: four Anglo-Mysore Wars (1767-1799) against Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan, ending with Tipu's death and a subsidiary alliance with the restored Wodeyars. Marathas: three Anglo-Maratha Wars (1775-1782, 1803-1805, 1817-1818); internal divisions after Nana Phadnavis's death and the Treaty of Bassein led to the end of Maratha power.

Punjab: after Ranjit Singh's death (1839), instability led to two Anglo-Sikh wars and annexation in 1849. Awadh: subjected to subsidiary treaties and territorial cessions (1801) and annexed in 1856. Other annexations: Sindh (1843, by Charles Napier - 'Peccavi'), Burma (wars of 1824-1826 and 1852, annexation of Lower Burma; full annexation 1885), and states taken under the Doctrine of Lapse.

Methods: wars, diplomacy, the Subsidiary Alliance, the Doctrine of Lapse, annexation on grounds of misgovernment, and exploiting rivalries among Indian powers. Reasons for success: military superiority (discipline, artillery, sepoy armies), financial resources, naval power, the lack of unity among Indian states and able leaders such as Clive, Hastings, Cornwallis, Wellesley, Hastings (Moira) and Dalhousie. By 1857, the Company ruled or controlled almost all of India.
section-123: Subsidiary Alliance (Wellesley): Indian rulers accepted British troops, a Resident, and British control over foreign relations, paying subsidies or ceding territory. It turned states into dependencies (Hyderabad, Mysore, Awadh, the Peshwa) and gave the British a large army at Indian expense. Doctrine of Lapse (Dalhousie): states without natural heirs were annexed (Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur). Annexation on grounds of misgovernment (Awadh, 1856) completed British expansion.

Administrative changes: Clive's Dual System (1765-1772) gave the Company revenue power without responsibility, leading to misrule and the 1770 famine. The Regulating Act (1773) created the Governor-General of Bengal and the Supreme Court at Calcutta and began parliamentary control. Pitt's India Act (1784) set up the Board of Control. Charter Acts: 1793 (renewal), 1813 (end of trade monopoly except tea and China trade, entry of missionaries, education grant), 1833 (end of commercial functions, Governor-General of India, centralised legislation, law commission under Macaulay), 1853 (separate legislative council, open competition for civil service).

Other reforms: Cornwallis's Permanent Settlement (1793), civil service and judicial reforms (the Cornwallis Code); Bentinck's social reforms (abolition of sati, 1829) and English education (Macaulay's Minute, 1835); Dalhousie's railways (1853), telegraph and postal reforms. These changes centralised authority and prepared the structure of later colonial government.
section-124: Causes: political (annexations, insult to the Mughals), economic (land revenue, ruin of crafts, loss of taluqdars' rights), social and religious (fear of conversion and interference), and military (sepoy grievances and greased cartridges). Course: Mangal Pandey at Barrackpore (29 March 1857); the outbreak at Meerut (10 May) and the march to Delhi; risings at Kanpur (Nana Saheb, Tantia Tope), Lucknow (Begum Hazrat Mahal), Jhansi (Rani Lakshmibai), Bihar (Kunwar Singh), Bareilly (Khan Bahadur Khan) and Faizabad (Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah). The British recaptured Delhi in September 1857 and other centres in 1858.

Nature: interpretations range from 'sepoy mutiny' (British view) to 'first war of independence' (Savarkar), a feudal reaction, or a popular revolt with peasant participation (Stokes, Mukherjee, Guha). The best view is that it began as a military mutiny but became a widespread popular rebellion in some regions, with Hindu-Muslim unity and anti-British feeling, though not nationalism in the modern sense.

Failure and consequences: limited geographical spread, lack of unified leadership and plan, the loyalty of many princes and the educated class, and superior British resources led to defeat. The Government of India Act 1858 transferred power to the Crown; Queen Victoria's Proclamation promised no annexations and religious non-interference; the army was reorganised on 'divide and rule' lines; and the British became cautious about social reforms and allied with princes and landlords. The revolt left a legacy that inspired later nationalists.
section-127: The term 'Middle Ages' (medium aevum) was coined by Renaissance humanists who saw the period between classical antiquity and their own revival of learning as a 'dark' middle period. Modern historians reject the idea of a 'Dark Age' and see the period as one of creativity and change. It is usually divided into the Early Middle Ages (c. 300/500-1000), the High or Central Middle Ages (c. 1000-1300) and the Late Middle Ages (c. 1300-1500).

Key themes include the transformation of the Roman world, the rise of Christianity and the Church, the barbarian kingdoms, the Carolingian empire, feudalism and manorialism, the revival of trade and towns, the Crusades, universities, and the crises of the fourteenth century. The period ended with the Renaissance, the fall of Constantinople (1453), the printing press and the voyages of discovery (1492).
section-128: The traditional date for the fall of the Western Empire is 476 CE, when the Germanic general Odoacer deposed the last emperor, Romulus Augustulus, and sent the imperial insignia to Constantinople. Causes discussed by historians include: political instability and civil wars; the division of the empire (395 CE, after Theodosius); economic problems (heavy taxation, inflation, decline of trade); dependence on Germanic soldiers; pressure from the Huns, which pushed Goths and others into the empire; and military defeats such as Adrianople (378), the sack of Rome by Alaric's Visigoths (410) and the Vandals (455).

Edward Gibbon ('The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire', 1776-1788) blamed Christianity and the loss of civic virtue. Modern historians such as Peter Brown speak of 'transformation' in 'Late Antiquity' rather than fall, emphasising continuities in law, language, the Church and urban life, while others (Bryan Ward-Perkins) stress real economic decline and violence.
section-129: Migration (the Völkerwanderung, or 'migration period') from the fourth to sixth centuries brought Goths, Vandals, Franks, Burgundians, Angles, Saxons, Lombards and others into Roman territory. The arrival of the Huns from the steppes around 370 CE pushed many groups westward.

Ethnogenesis means the formation of an ethnic identity. Historians such as Herwig Wolfram and Patrick Geary argue that 'barbarian' peoples were not ancient, fixed tribes but new groups formed during the migrations by combining various peoples under successful leaders and around shared traditions, laws and myths. For example, the Goths included people of different origins. Identities were flexible and politically constructed, a view that challenges older nationalist histories.
section-130: Major successor kingdoms: the Visigoths in Spain (capital Toledo), the Ostrogoths in Italy under Theodoric (493-526), the Vandals in North Africa (Carthage), the Burgundians in eastern Gaul, the Franks in Gaul under Clovis (481-511) of the Merovingian dynasty, who converted to Catholic Christianity (c. 496), the Anglo-Saxons in England, and later the Lombards in Italy (568).

These kingdoms combined Germanic traditions (warrior bands, kingship based on military leadership, customary law such as the Salic Law of the Franks) with Roman institutions (Latin, Roman law for Roman subjects, bishops and the Church, cities). Many rulers were initially Arian Christians, which created tension with Catholic subjects. The Frankish kingdom, being Catholic, became the most successful.
section-131: The Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire, with its capital at Constantinople, survived until 1453. It was Greek-speaking, Christian (Orthodox), and governed by an emperor considered God's representative on earth, with an elaborate bureaucracy, a professional army and strong fortifications (the Theodosian Walls). Its economy was based on trade and a stable gold currency (the solidus or bezant).

Justinian I (527-565) reconquered North Africa, Italy and part of Spain, compiled the Corpus Juris Civilis and built Hagia Sophia. Later the empire lost territory to the Persians, Arabs (Syria, Egypt, North Africa in the seventh century) and Slavs, and was weakened by the iconoclasm controversy (726-843) and the Fourth Crusade's sack of Constantinople (1204). The Ottoman Turks captured Constantinople in 1453. Byzantium preserved Greek learning and influenced Russia and the Slavic world.
section-132: After Constantine and Theodosius, the Church became the most important institution in western Europe. It was organised in dioceses under bishops, with the Bishop of Rome (the Pope) claiming leadership as successor of St Peter. Pope Leo I (440-461) asserted papal primacy and Pope Gregory I (590-604) organised papal estates, sent missionaries to England (Augustine of Canterbury, 597) and strengthened the papacy.

Church Fathers such as St Augustine of Hippo ('City of God', 'Confessions'), St Jerome (Latin Vulgate Bible) and St Ambrose shaped Christian doctrine. The Church preserved literacy, Latin and classical learning through its clergy and monasteries, converted the barbarian peoples, provided social services, and gave legitimacy to kings. It also became a major landowner.
section-133: Pope Gelasius I (494) formulated the 'two swords' theory: spiritual authority belonged to the Church and temporal authority to the emperor, but the spiritual was superior. The papacy allied with the Franks: Pepin the Short was anointed king (751-754) and gave the Pope lands in central Italy (the 'Donation of Pepin', basis of the Papal States); Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor on Christmas Day 800. Otto I was crowned Holy Roman Emperor in 962.

The conflict reached its height in the Investiture Controversy (1075-1122) over who should appoint bishops: Pope Gregory VII excommunicated Emperor Henry IV, who did penance at Canossa (1077). The Concordat of Worms (1122) was a compromise. Later conflicts involved Frederick Barbarossa and Frederick II against the popes, and Boniface VIII against Philip IV of France ('Unam Sanctam', 1302, claiming papal supremacy). The relationship shaped ideas of church-state separation.
section-134: Christian monasticism began in Egypt with hermits like St Anthony and communal monasteries under Pachomius. In the West, St Benedict of Nursia founded Monte Cassino (c. 529) and wrote the Rule of St Benedict, prescribing a balanced life of prayer (the divine office), manual labour and study under an abbot, with vows of poverty, chastity and obedience ('Ora et labora' - pray and work). Irish monks (St Columba, Columbanus) spread Christianity and learning.

Monasteries copied manuscripts in their scriptoria, preserving classical and Christian texts; ran schools; cleared forests and developed agriculture; provided hospitality, charity and medical care; and became major landowners. Reform movements arose when monasteries became wealthy and lax: Cluny (910), the Cistercians (Citeaux, 1098; St Bernard of Clairvaux), and later the mendicant (begging) friars - Franciscans (St Francis of Assisi, 1209) and Dominicans (St Dominic, 1216).
section-135: After the Prophet Muhammad's death (632), the Arabs under the caliphs conquered Syria, Palestine, Egypt and Persia within twenty years, then North Africa, and Spain (from 711), until they were stopped by Charles Martel at the Battle of Tours/Poitiers (732). The Umayyad caliphate (Damascus, 661-750) was followed by the Abbasids (Baghdad, 750-1258); an Umayyad emirate (later caliphate) continued in Córdoba, Spain.

The Belgian historian Henri Pirenne ('Mohammed and Charlemagne', 1937) argued that the Arab conquests, rather than the barbarian invasions, ended the unity of the Mediterranean world and its trade, turning western Europe inward towards an agrarian economy: 'Without Muhammad, Charlemagne would be inconceivable.' Later archaeology modified his thesis, showing trade continued. Islamic civilisation preserved and developed Greek philosophy, mathematics, medicine and astronomy, which later reached Europe through Spain and Sicily.
section-136: In the Frankish kingdoms, power depended on military force and land. The Merovingian kings (from Clovis) granted land to their warriors and nobles, weakening royal power; real power passed to the 'mayors of the palace'. Charles Martel, mayor of the palace, defeated the Arabs at Tours (732) and rewarded his followers with land (often taken from the Church) in exchange for military service, especially as mounted warriors.

Aristocratic families controlled large estates worked by dependent peasants and slaves, built followings of armed men (vassals) bound by oaths of loyalty, and competed for royal favour, offices and land. Historians debate how far this produced 'feudalism' - the system of lords, vassals and fiefs - which historians such as Susan Reynolds ('Fiefs and Vassals', 1994) argue was much less systematic than once believed.
section-137: Early medieval exchange included local markets, regional trade and long-distance trade in luxury goods (silk, spices, slaves, furs, amber) through Mediterranean, North Sea and Baltic routes. Emporia (trading towns) such as Dorestad (Netherlands), Quentovic, Hamwic (Southampton) and Hedeby (Denmark) flourished in the seventh to ninth centuries. Vikings combined raiding with trade from the Baltic to Byzantium and the Caliphate. Charlemagne introduced the silver penny (denier).

Gift exchange was central to social and political relationships: kings gave land, treasure, weapons and feasts to followers to secure loyalty, and received gifts in return; diplomatic gifts were exchanged between rulers (Harun al-Rashid's elephant for Charlemagne). Anthropologist Marcel Mauss's 'The Gift' (1925) showed that gifts create obligations. Historians such as Philip Grierson and Georges Duby emphasised the importance of gift-giving in the early medieval economy alongside commerce.
section-138: Pepin the Short, son of Charles Martel, deposed the last Merovingian king and became king of the Franks (751), with papal approval, founding the Carolingian dynasty. His son Charlemagne (Charles the Great, r. 768-814) conquered the Lombard kingdom in Italy (774), the Saxons (after brutal wars, forcing their conversion), Bavaria and the Avars, and fought the Muslims in Spain (the 'Song of Roland' is based on the battle of Roncesvalles, 778). His empire covered most of western and central Europe, with Aachen as capital.

He was crowned Emperor of the Romans by Pope Leo III on Christmas Day 800. He governed through counts, inspected by royal agents (missi dominici), and issued capitularies (decrees). The 'Carolingian Renaissance' revived learning, with the scholar Alcuin of York at his palace school, the reform of the Church, the copying of manuscripts and the new Carolingian minuscule script.
section-139: Charlemagne's empire was divided among his grandsons by the Treaty of Verdun (843) into West Francia (the origin of France), East Francia (the origin of Germany) and Middle Francia (Lotharingia, between them). Viking, Magyar and Muslim raids and weak rulers caused the decline of royal power, and local lords became stronger.

His legacy: the idea of a Christian empire allied with the papacy, revived by Otto I as the Holy Roman Empire (962-1806); the Carolingian Renaissance's preservation of classical texts (most surviving Latin classics come from Carolingian copies) and its script, which is the basis of modern lower-case letters; the model of a Christian king ruling with the Church; and the foundation of the later states of France and Germany. Charlemagne is sometimes called the 'Father of Europe'.
section-140: After the Romans left Britain (c. 410), Anglo-Saxon kingdoms formed - the 'Heptarchy' of Northumbria, Mercia, Wessex, East Anglia, Essex, Sussex and Kent. Christianity spread through Augustine's mission (597) and Irish monks; the Venerable Bede wrote the 'Ecclesiastical History of the English People' (731). Viking invasions from the late eighth century led to the Danelaw, but Alfred the Great of Wessex (871-899) resisted the Danes, built fortified towns (burhs), promoted learning in English and laid foundations for a unified kingdom achieved by his successors (Athelstan, 927).

The Norman Conquest (1066), when William the Conqueror defeated Harold at Hastings, introduced Norman feudalism, French culture, castles, the Domesday Book (1086, a survey of land and resources) and a strong monarchy. Henry II (1154-1189) developed common law and royal courts. King John was forced to accept the Magna Carta (1215), which limited royal power. Parliament developed in the thirteenth century (Simon de Montfort's parliament, 1265; Edward I's 'Model Parliament', 1295).
section-141: Europe's population may have doubled or tripled between 1000 and 1300, from perhaps 35-40 million to about 70-80 million. Causes included the end of Viking, Magyar and Muslim invasions, a warmer climate (the 'Medieval Warm Period'), and agricultural improvements: the heavy wheeled plough (carruca) for the heavy soils of northern Europe; the horse collar and horseshoes, allowing horses to plough; the three-field rotation system (one field in winter crops, one in spring crops, one fallow), which increased production; and water mills and windmills.

Peasants cleared forests, drained marshes (in Flanders and the Netherlands) and colonised new lands, especially the German eastward expansion (Ostsiedlung). Increased food production supported population growth, the growth of towns and trade, and the expansion of Europe in the Crusades and Reconquista.
section-142: The idealised medieval view divided society into three orders: those who pray (oratores - clergy), those who fight (bellatores - knights and nobles) and those who work (laboratores - peasants), as described by Bishop Adalbero of Laon (c. 1020). Knights were mounted warriors bound to lords by homage and fealty, receiving fiefs (land) in return for military service. Chivalry developed as a code of conduct emphasising bravery, loyalty, piety and protection of the weak, influenced by the Church and courtly literature.

Most peasants lived on manors controlled by lords. Serfs were bound to the land and owed labour services (working on the lord's demesne), dues in kind or cash, and payments for using the lord's mill, oven and press (banalities); they were subject to the lord's court. Free peasants paid rent. Peasants' lives were hard, but they had customary rights. Historians emphasise that real social relations varied greatly across regions and over time.
section-143: The Gregorian Reform (eleventh century), named after Pope Gregory VII (1073-1085), aimed to free the Church from lay control, end simony (buying of church offices) and enforce clerical celibacy. Gregory's 'Dictatus Papae' claimed that the Pope could depose emperors. The College of Cardinals was given the right to elect popes (1059). The Investiture Controversy followed.

The papacy reached its height under Innocent III (1198-1216), who intervened in the affairs of England (forcing King John to become his vassal), France and the Holy Roman Empire, launched the Fourth Crusade and the Albigensian Crusade against the Cathar heretics, and held the Fourth Lateran Council (1215), which defined doctrine (transubstantiation) and required annual confession. The papacy developed a bureaucracy, canon law, taxation and the Inquisition (from 1231). Its claims declined after Boniface VIII's conflict with Philip IV.
section-144: Pope Urban II called the First Crusade at the Council of Clermont (1095), after the Byzantine emperor Alexios I asked for help against the Seljuk Turks, who had defeated the Byzantines at Manzikert (1071). Crusaders were promised remission of sins. The First Crusade (1096-1099) captured Jerusalem (1099) with great massacres and established Crusader states: Jerusalem, Edessa, Antioch and Tripoli. Military orders (Templars, Hospitallers) were formed.

Later crusades: the Second (1147-1149) failed after the fall of Edessa; Saladin recaptured Jerusalem (1187) after the battle of Hattin; the Third Crusade (1189-1192) of Richard the Lionheart, Philip II and Frederick Barbarossa won coastal cities but not Jerusalem; the Fourth (1202-1204) sacked Constantinople. The last Crusader stronghold, Acre, fell in 1291. Effects: increased trade with the East (benefiting Venice and Genoa), cultural contact, strengthening of papal and royal power, persecution of Jews, deepening of the split between the Latin and Orthodox churches and lasting hostility between Christians and Muslims.
section-145: Robert S. Lopez ('The Commercial Revolution of the Middle Ages, 950-1350') described the transformation of the European economy. Italian cities (Venice, Genoa, Pisa) dominated Mediterranean trade with the Byzantine and Islamic worlds, importing spices, silk and luxury goods. In the north, Flanders produced woollen cloth from English wool, and the Hanseatic League (from the thirteenth century), a confederation of German towns such as Lübeck and Hamburg, controlled Baltic and North Sea trade.

The Champagne fairs in France connected Italian and northern merchants. New business techniques included partnerships (commenda), bills of exchange, banking (the Medici, Bardi and Peruzzi of Florence), double-entry bookkeeping, insurance and new gold coins (the Florentine florin, 1252, and the Venetian ducat). Improvements in roads, ships and navigation (the compass) helped, and the countryside became more commercialised as peasants paid money rents and sold produce in towns.
section-146: Universities (universitas, meaning a guild or corporation) developed from cathedral schools in the twelfth century. Bologna (c. 1088) was famous for law, organised by students; Paris (c. 1150-1200) for theology, organised by masters; and Oxford (c. 1167) and Cambridge (1209) followed. Others included Salerno (medicine), Montpellier, Padua and Salamanca. By 1500 there were about eighty universities.

Students studied the seven liberal arts - the trivium (grammar, rhetoric, logic) and quadrivium (arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, music) - before higher faculties of theology, law and medicine. Teaching used lectures and disputations in Latin. Scholasticism tried to reconcile faith and reason using Aristotle's works (reintroduced through Arabic translations and commentaries of Avicenna and Averroes); key scholars were Peter Abelard ('Sic et Non') and Thomas Aquinas ('Summa Theologica'). Universities trained clergy, lawyers, doctors and officials.
section-147: Towns grew from the eleventh century around castles, monasteries, old Roman sites, river crossings and markets, due to population growth, agricultural surplus and trade. Towns obtained charters from lords or kings granting rights of self-government, markets and freedom for inhabitants ('town air makes free' - a serf who lived in a town for a year and a day became free). Merchants and craftsmen formed guilds that regulated prices, quality, training (apprentice, journeyman, master) and protected members.

Major urban centres included Venice, Florence, Milan, Paris, London, Bruges, Ghent and Cologne. Towns created a new social group, the burghers or bourgeoisie, and led to conflicts with lords and between rich patricians and poorer artisans (the Ciompi revolt in Florence, 1378). Towns were centres of trade, crafts, education, cathedral-building (Gothic architecture) and new religious movements, and they laid the basis of modern urban society.
section-148: The fourteenth century saw a series of disasters: the Great Famine (1315-1317) caused by cold, wet weather (the beginning of the 'Little Ice Age'), the Black Death (1347-1351), a plague brought from Central Asia via the Black Sea to Italy, which killed about one-third to one-half of Europe's population, and recurrent plagues afterwards. The Hundred Years' War between England and France (1337-1453), with battles such as Crécy (1346), Poitiers (1356) and Agincourt (1415) and Joan of Arc's role (1429-1431), caused devastation.

Consequences: labour shortages raised wages and weakened serfdom; peasants revolted (the Jacquerie in France, 1358; the English Peasants' Revolt of 1381 under Wat Tyler against the poll tax); towns saw workers' revolts; Jews were persecuted as scapegoats; religious anxiety grew (flagellants); and the Church's prestige declined. Some historians see the crisis as a turning point that destroyed the medieval order and prepared the way for the Renaissance and new economic systems.
section-149: The 'Babylonian Captivity' (1309-1377): after the conflict between Boniface VIII and Philip IV, the papacy moved to Avignon in France, where seven French popes lived under French influence. When Pope Gregory XI returned to Rome (1377), the subsequent election in 1378 led to two rival popes - Urban VI in Rome and Clement VII in Avignon. This Great Western Schism (1378-1417) divided Europe: France, Scotland and others supported Avignon, England and the Holy Roman Empire supported Rome. In 1409, the Council of Pisa added a third pope.

The conciliar movement held that a general council of the Church had authority over the Pope. The Council of Constance (1414-1418) ended the schism by deposing or accepting the resignation of the rival popes and electing Martin V; it also condemned and burned the Czech reformer Jan Hus. The Schism damaged papal prestige and encouraged critics such as John Wycliffe in England and Hus, foreshadowing the Reformation.
section-150: Humanism was an intellectual movement that emphasised the study of classical Latin and Greek literature (the studia humanitatis - grammar, rhetoric, poetry, history and moral philosophy) and the dignity and potential of human beings. It began in fourteenth-century Italy with Francesco Petrarch (1304-1374), the 'father of humanism', who searched for classical manuscripts and wrote in Latin and Italian, and Giovanni Boccaccio ('Decameron'). Dante Alighieri's 'Divine Comedy' (early fourteenth century) is often seen as a bridge.

Later humanists included Coluccio Salutati and Leonardo Bruni (civic humanism in Florence), Lorenzo Valla (who proved that the 'Donation of Constantine' was a forgery), and the revival of Greek after Byzantine scholars came to Italy (Manuel Chrysoloras; the Council of Florence, 1439; the fall of Constantinople, 1453). The invention of printing by Johannes Gutenberg (c. 1450) spread humanist ideas. Humanism led to the Renaissance and influenced the Reformation (Erasmus).
section-152: Transformation of the Roman world: the Western Empire faced political instability, economic difficulties and pressure from migrating peoples (Goths, Vandals, Franks, Anglo-Saxons), culminating in the deposition of Romulus Augustulus (476). Historians debate 'fall' (Gibbon, Ward-Perkins) versus 'transformation' (Peter Brown's Late Antiquity). Ethnogenesis theory argues that barbarian peoples formed new identities during migration. Barbarian kingdoms (Visigoths, Ostrogoths, Vandals, Franks, Lombards, Anglo-Saxons) combined Germanic and Roman traditions; Clovis's Catholic conversion made the Franks dominant.

Eastern Roman Empire: survived with its capital at Constantinople, a centralised state and Orthodox Christianity; Justinian's reconquests, legal code and Hagia Sophia; later losses to the Arabs. Church and monasticism: the papacy (Leo I, Gregory I) grew in authority; the theory of two swords (Gelasius); Benedictine monasticism preserved learning and developed agriculture; Irish and Anglo-Saxon missionaries converted northern Europe. The alliance of popes and Frankish kings (Pepin, Charlemagne) shaped medieval politics.

Islam: the Arab conquests (seventh-eighth centuries) took the southern and eastern Mediterranean and Spain, stopped at Tours (732). Pirenne argued this divided the Mediterranean and shifted Europe's centre northward. Islamic civilisation preserved Greek learning that later revived European thought. The Early Middle Ages thus saw the creation of three civilisations - Latin Christian, Byzantine and Islamic - from the Roman world.
section-153: Early medieval society: warrior aristocrats controlled land and dependent peasants; kings rewarded followers with land and gifts; Charles Martel used land grants to build cavalry. Exchange included local markets, emporia trading towns, Viking networks and gift-giving that created loyalty and obligations. Carolingian empire: Charlemagne's conquests, coronation (800), administration through counts and missi dominici, and the Carolingian Renaissance (Alcuin, minuscule script). The Treaty of Verdun (843) divided the empire, and Viking, Magyar and Saracen invasions encouraged local lordship.

Kingdoms and principalities 1000-1300: the Capetian kings of France (from 987) gradually extended royal power (Philip II Augustus); the Holy Roman Empire (from 962) struggled with the papacy and local princes; England developed a strong monarchy after 1066 (Domesday Book, common law under Henry II, Magna Carta 1215, Parliament); the Christian kingdoms of Spain advanced in the Reconquista. Feudal relations (lords, vassals, fiefs) and manorialism (lords and serfs) organised society, though historians debate how systematic feudalism was.

Economic growth: agricultural innovations (heavy plough, horse collar, three-field rotation, mills), forest clearance and colonisation, a warmer climate and peace led to population growth, which in turn stimulated the commercial revolution, urban growth and cultural flowering of the High Middle Ages.
section-154: Religious reform: the Cluniac reform (from 910) and Gregorian reform (eleventh century) fought simony, lay investiture and clerical marriage; the Investiture Controversy (Gregory VII vs Henry IV, Canossa 1077, Concordat of Worms 1122); papal monarchy under Innocent III (Fourth Lateran Council, 1215); new orders - Cistercians, and the mendicant Franciscans and Dominicans who preached in towns; and campaigns against heresy (the Cathars, the Inquisition).

Expansion: the Crusades (1095-1291) established Crusader states in the Levant and colonies of Italian merchants; the Reconquista in Spain (Toledo 1085, Las Navas de Tolosa 1212); German eastward settlement; and the Normans in Sicily and southern Italy. Commercial revolution: Italian trade with the East, Flemish cloth industry, the Champagne fairs, the Hanseatic League, banking, bills of exchange and gold coins, and the commercialisation of the countryside.

Universities and towns: Bologna, Paris and Oxford became centres of learning; scholasticism (Abelard, Aquinas) combined Christian theology with Aristotle; Gothic cathedrals (Chartres, Notre-Dame) expressed religious and urban pride. Towns obtained charters, guilds organised economic life, and a bourgeoisie emerged. Late medieval humanism (Petrarch, Boccaccio, Bruni) began to revive classical learning. The Central Middle Ages were therefore a period of growth, confidence and creativity.
section-155: Crisis: the Great Famine (1315-1317), the Black Death (1347-1351, killing a third or more of the population) and recurring plagues, and the Hundred Years' War (1337-1453) devastated Europe. Economic contraction, abandonment of villages, labour shortages and higher wages followed; lords tried to keep wages low (the Statute of Labourers, 1351, in England), leading to revolts such as the Jacquerie (1358), the English Peasants' Revolt (1381) and the Ciompi revolt (1378). Serfdom declined in western Europe but strengthened in eastern Europe.

State consolidation: the monarchies of France (after the Hundred Years' War), England (after the Wars of the Roses, 1455-1485, under the Tudors), and Spain (union of Castile and Aragon through Ferdinand and Isabella, 1469; conquest of Granada, 1492) became stronger, with standing armies, taxation and bureaucracies. The Ottomans captured Constantinople (1453).

Church crisis: the Avignon papacy (1309-1377), the Great Schism (1378-1417) and the conciliar movement (Councils of Constance and Basel) weakened papal authority. Critics such as John Wycliffe (Lollards) and Jan Hus (Hussites) attacked church corruption. At the same time, humanism, printing (Gutenberg, c. 1450) and the voyages of discovery (Columbus, 1492; Vasco da Gama, 1498) marked the transition to the early modern age.
section-158: Environmental history emerged as a field in the 1970s, especially in the USA, influenced by the environmental movement (Rachel Carson's 'Silent Spring', 1962, about pesticides). Pioneers include Donald Worster ('Dust Bowl', 1979), William Cronon ('Changes in the Land', 1983), Alfred Crosby ('The Columbian Exchange', 1972, 'Ecological Imperialism', 1986) and, in France, the Annales school (Fernand Braudel, Emmanuel Le Roy Ladurie on climate history).

Worster described three levels: (1) the study of nature itself in the past (ecosystems, climate); (2) the socio-economic realm, how people used and changed the environment through technology and production; and (3) the realm of ideas, perceptions, ethics and laws about nature. In India, Madhav Gadgil and Ramachandra Guha ('This Fissured Land', 1992), Ramachandra Guha ('The Unquiet Woods', 1989) and Mahesh Rangarajan are key environmental historians.
section-159: Environmental history uses evidence and methods from many disciplines: ecology (ecosystems, food chains, biodiversity), geography (landscapes, climate, soils), geology, botany and zoology (pollen analysis, tree rings - dendrochronology - and ice cores to reconstruct past climates), anthropology (how communities use resources and their beliefs about nature), economics, sociology, archaeology and political science.

This approach helps explain, for example, how deforestation affected rainfall and soil erosion, how diseases spread with colonial conquest (the Columbian Exchange), and how famine was linked to both climate (El Niño droughts) and colonial policy (Mike Davis, 'Late Victorian Holocausts', 2001). It also uses traditional historical sources - government records, travellers' accounts, forest department reports, folk songs and oral histories.
section-160: The term 'ecology' was coined by the German biologist Ernst Haeckel in 1866 (from Greek oikos, household). An ecosystem consists of living organisms (biotic components - producers, consumers, decomposers) and their physical environment (abiotic - air, water, soil, sunlight) interacting through energy flows and nutrient cycles. Key concepts include carrying capacity, biodiversity, ecological balance, succession and the food chain.

The environment includes all natural and human-made surroundings. Environmental historians use ecological concepts to understand how human actions - hunting, farming, deforestation, irrigation, industry and urbanisation - changed ecosystems, and how environmental changes in turn affected societies. Ecology also inspired philosophies such as 'deep ecology' (Arne Naess), which values nature for its own sake.
section-161: The United Nations Conference on the Human Environment was held in Stockholm, Sweden, from 5 to 16 June 1972 - the first major global conference on the environment. India's Prime Minister Indira Gandhi spoke, famously linking poverty and environment ('Are not poverty and need the greatest polluters?'). 5 June is celebrated as World Environment Day.

The Stockholm Declaration contained 26 principles, including the human right to a healthy environment, the responsibility to protect and improve the environment for present and future generations, the conservation of natural resources and wildlife, the control of pollution, and the sovereign right of states to exploit their resources without causing damage to others. It led to the creation of the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP, headquartered in Nairobi). Later milestones include the Brundtland Report (1987, 'sustainable development'), the Rio Earth Summit (1992), the Kyoto Protocol (1997) and the Paris Agreement (2015). In India, the Department of Environment (1980), the Water Act (1974), the Air Act (1981) and the Environment (Protection) Act (1986) followed.
section-162: For most of human history (over 95 percent), people lived by hunting animals, fishing and gathering wild plants, fruits, nuts and roots. Hunter-gatherers lived in small, mobile bands, moving with the seasons and the availability of resources. They had detailed knowledge of their environment and generally had a relatively low impact on it.

However, they did change environments: they used fire to clear vegetation and drive game, and some historians argue that early humans contributed to the extinction of large animals (megafauna) in Australia and the Americas ('Pleistocene overkill' theory). Anthropologist Marshall Sahlins called hunter-gatherers 'the original affluent society' because their needs were few and easily met. In India, some communities such as the Chenchus, Birhors and the Andaman islanders continued hunting-gathering into modern times.
section-163: Pastoralism developed after the domestication of animals (sheep, goats, cattle, camels, horses, yaks, reindeer). Pastoral nomads move with their herds in search of pasture and water, often following seasonal patterns (transhumance - moving between summer pastures in the mountains and winter pastures in the plains). Examples include the Mongols and other steppe peoples, the Bedouins of Arabia, the Maasai of East Africa and, in India, the Gujjars and Bakarwals of Jammu and Kashmir, the Gaddis of Himachal Pradesh, the Raikas (Rebaris) of Rajasthan and the Dhangars of Maharashtra.

Pastoralism allowed people to use dry grasslands and mountains unsuitable for farming. Overgrazing could cause land degradation, but pastoralists also had traditional systems to manage pastures. Relations with farmers included both exchange (manure for crops) and conflict. Colonial rule restricted pastoral movement through forest laws, grazing taxes and the Criminal Tribes Act (1871), which labelled some nomadic groups as criminals.
section-164: The Neolithic Revolution, beginning around 10,000 years ago in the Fertile Crescent of West Asia and independently in China, Mesoamerica, the Andes, New Guinea and parts of Africa and India, led to farming and permanent villages. Agriculture produced surplus food, supported larger populations, cities, states, social classes, writing and specialisation.

It also transformed environments: forests were cleared, land was ploughed, rivers were diverted for irrigation, and wild plants and animals were replaced by domesticated ones. Environmental problems included soil erosion, salinisation of irrigated land (contributing to the decline of Mesopotamian agriculture), deforestation and new diseases from living close to animals. Historians such as Jared Diamond ('Guns, Germs, and Steel', 1997) called agriculture 'the worst mistake in the history of the human race' in terms of health and inequality, although this view is debated.
section-165: The Industrial Revolution, beginning in Britain around 1760, used fossil fuels - coal, and later oil and gas - to power machines, factories, railways and steamships. It led to rapid urbanisation, population growth, mass production and consumption. Environmental effects included air pollution (smog in London; the 1952 Great Smog killed thousands), water pollution, deforestation, mining damage, loss of biodiversity and the rise of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, causing global warming.

In the twentieth century, chemicals (DDT, as exposed in 'Silent Spring'), nuclear technology, plastics and industrial agriculture created new problems. Industrial disasters such as the Bhopal gas tragedy (December 1984, the Union Carbide methyl isocyanate leak that killed thousands) and Chernobyl (1986) showed the dangers. Scientists now speak of the 'Anthropocene', a geological age in which humans are the main force changing the planet. Climate change is the most serious environmental crisis of our time.
section-166: Before colonial rule, Indian forests were used by many communities - tribal groups practising shifting cultivation, hunting and gathering, pastoralists, peasants who collected fuel, fodder and timber, and artisans who used forest products. Use was regulated by local customs and community institutions; sacred groves (devrais in Maharashtra, kavus in Kerala, the sacred forests of Mawphlang in Meghalaya) were protected, and in Mizoram village chiefs set aside protected forest land around villages.

Rulers also used forests for hunting, elephants and timber, and sometimes cleared them for agriculture and revenue. Madhav Gadgil and Ramachandra Guha argued that pre-colonial India had relatively sustainable resource use with community control; critics (for example, Sumit Guha) argue that pre-colonial states also exploited forests and that the picture should not be idealised. Nonetheless, colonial rule marked a major break by asserting state monopoly over forests.
section-167: The British saw India's forests primarily as a commercial resource. Initially, they cleared forests for agriculture to increase land revenue and for plantations (tea in Assam and the Nilgiris, coffee, indigo). From the mid-nineteenth century, timber was in great demand, and forests were rapidly depleted. Valuable species such as teak, sal, deodar and sandalwood were exploited.

Wildlife was also exploited: colonial officials and princes hunted tigers, leopards and elephants on a massive scale, and rewards were given for killing 'vermin' (tigers, wolves); tens of thousands of tigers were killed between 1875 and 1925. Mining (coal, iron, manganese) and the extension of commercial agriculture also transformed landscapes. Colonial resource exploitation thus served imperial economic and strategic needs.
section-168: In the early nineteenth century, oak forests in England were depleted, and the Royal Navy needed timber for ships. Indian teak from Malabar and Burma was strong and durable, and large quantities were cut; the British built ships in Bombay and elsewhere. The first teak plantation was established at Nilambur in Kerala (1840s) by H. V. Conolly.

From the 1850s, the railways created huge demand for wooden sleepers - each mile of track needed about 1,760-2,000 sleepers - and for fuel wood for locomotives. By the 1890s, about a million sleepers were required every year. Forests around railway lines in the Himalayas, central India and the south were cleared. Lord Dalhousie's 1855 forest charter and the concern about forest destruction led to the creation of the Forest Department.
section-169: During the First World War (1914-1918) and the Second World War (1939-1945), the British needed huge amounts of timber for military purposes - for ships, railway sleepers, ammunition boxes, aircraft, buildings, fuel and paper. The Forest Department increased cutting far beyond sustainable levels, especially in the Himalayan forests, central India and Burma.

War also increased demand for bamboo, resin, tannins and other forest products, and in the Second World War, north-east India and Burma became war zones (the Imphal and Kohima battles of 1944), leading to clearance of forests for roads and camps. After the wars, forests were seriously degraded. The wars thus linked local environments to the global imperial war economy.
section-170: In 1864, the Imperial Forest Department was established with the German forester Dietrich Brandis as the first Inspector-General of Forests. The Indian Forest Act of 1865 was followed by the more comprehensive Indian Forest Act of 1878, which classified forests into three categories: reserved forests (the best, where villagers had almost no rights), protected forests (with some customary rights recorded and regulated) and village forests. The Indian Forest Act of 1927 consolidated these laws. The Forest Research Institute was set up at Dehradun (1906).

Effects: forest communities lost access to forests for fuel, fodder, grazing, food and timber; shifting cultivation (jhum, podu, bewar) was restricted or banned; hunting was prohibited for villagers while it remained a sport for elites; forest officials and guards harassed villagers; and many forest-dwellers became labourers for the forest department. This led to resistance, such as the Bastar rebellion (1910), the revolts in Kumaon and Garhwal (forest fires, 1916-1921), the Rampa rebellion of Alluri Sitarama Raju (1922-1924) in Andhra and forest satyagrahas during the national movement. After independence, the National Forest Policy (1952, 1988) and the Forest Rights Act (2006) tried to address these issues.
section-171: The Chipko ('to hug' or 'to stick') movement began in 1973 at Mandal village in Chamoli district, Garhwal (now Uttarakhand), when villagers led by Chandi Prasad Bhatt of the Dasholi Gram Swarajya Sangh prevented a sports goods company from cutting ash trees by threatening to hug them. In 1974, at Reni village, women led by Gaura Devi hugged trees to stop loggers while the men were away. The movement was inspired by Gandhian non-violence and the earlier sacrifice of the Bishnoi community at Khejarli (Rajasthan, 1730), when Amrita Devi and 363 people died protecting trees.

Sunderlal Bahuguna spread the movement through padyatras and the slogan 'Ecology is permanent economy'. In 1980, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi imposed a fifteen-year ban on commercial felling in the Himalayan forests of Uttar Pradesh. Chipko is significant as a peasant and women's movement for the right to use local resources, and it inspired the Appiko movement in Karnataka (1983). Ramachandra Guha's 'The Unquiet Woods' studied it.
section-172: The Sardar Sarovar Project on the Narmada river in Gujarat, part of a plan for about 30 large dams on the Narmada (in Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Gujarat), was intended to provide irrigation, drinking water (to Kutch and Saurashtra) and electricity. Critics pointed out that it would displace hundreds of thousands of people, mostly tribals and peasants, submerge forests and fertile land, and that resettlement was inadequate.

The Narmada Bachao Andolan (NBA, 'Save the Narmada Movement') was formed in 1989, led by Medha Patkar and supported by Baba Amte, Arundhati Roy and others. It used rallies, hunger strikes, jal samadhi (threatening to drown in rising waters) and court cases. The World Bank withdrew funding in 1993 after the Morse Committee's independent review. The Supreme Court allowed construction to continue in 2000 with conditions for rehabilitation; the dam was completed and inaugurated in 2017. The NBA raised fundamental questions about development, displacement and environmental justice.
section-173: Silent Valley in Palakkad district, Kerala, is one of the last undisturbed tropical evergreen rainforests in the Western Ghats, home to rare species such as the lion-tailed macaque. In the 1970s, the Kerala State Electricity Board proposed a hydroelectric dam on the Kunthipuzha river, which would submerge part of the forest.

The Kerala Sastra Sahitya Parishad (KSSP, a people's science movement), scientists (Salim Ali), poets (Sugathakumari, whose poem 'Marathinu Stuthi' - Ode to a Tree - became the movement's anthem), and international conservationists campaigned against it from 1973. Prime Minister Indira Gandhi intervened, and the project was dropped in 1983. Silent Valley was declared a National Park in 1984 (inaugurated 1985). It was one of India's first successful environmental campaigns and showed the role of scientists and citizens in conservation.
section-174: In 2000, Hindustan Coca-Cola Beverages set up a bottling plant at Plachimada in Palakkad district, Kerala. Local residents, mostly Dalit and Adivasi farmers and labourers, complained that the plant's extraction of groundwater dried up wells and that the remaining water became polluted; the company also distributed sludge as fertiliser, which was found to contain toxic heavy metals (cadmium and lead), according to a BBC report (2003).

Protests began in April 2002, led by Mylamma, an Adivasi woman, and others, with sit-ins outside the factory. The Perumatty gram panchayat cancelled the plant's licence (2003), leading to court cases on whether a local body can control groundwater use (the Kerala High Court initially supported the panchayat). The plant stopped production in 2004. In 2011 the Kerala Assembly passed a bill to set up a tribunal for compensation. The issue raised questions about corporate use of natural resources, groundwater as a common resource, and the rights of local communities.
section-175: Environmental historians and activists emphasise that environmental problems affect the poor and marginalised most severely - tribal communities displaced by dams, mines and wildlife sanctuaries, fishing communities affected by industrial pollution, pastoralists losing grazing land and poor urban residents living near polluted sites. Ramachandra Guha and Joan Martinez-Alier called this the 'environmentalism of the poor', which is about survival and livelihood rather than wilderness protection.

Movements such as Chipko, the NBA, the struggle of the Dongria Kondh against bauxite mining in the Niyamgiri hills (Odisha; the gram sabhas rejected Vedanta's project in 2013), and the Forest Rights Act (2006), which recognises the rights of forest-dwellers, show the voices of the margins. Environmental history aims to include these perspectives and to recognise indigenous knowledge of ecosystems.
section-176: Women in rural India often collect fuel, fodder and water, gather forest produce and manage household food, so deforestation and water scarcity increase their workload directly. This explains women's leadership in movements like Chipko (Gaura Devi), Plachimada (Mylamma) and the NBA (Medha Patkar).

Ecofeminism links the domination of women and nature by patriarchal and capitalist systems. Vandana Shiva ('Staying Alive', 1988) argued that women are closer to nature and protect it, and that Western development models destroy both. Critics such as Bina Agarwal proposed 'feminist environmentalism', arguing that women's relationship with nature comes from their material roles and social position, not from any inherent nature. Wangari Maathai's Green Belt Movement in Kenya (Nobel Peace Prize, 2004) is another example of women leading environmental action.
